old.text: Deleuze and Guattari's name, in Anti-Oedipus (1972), for desire as a process of production: an unconscious made of machines that couple flows and cut them, at work directly in natural and social production.
Anti-Oedipus opens by multiplying the unconscious.
old.note: No source frames the opening as multiplying the unconscious.

old.text: In place of a single id, Deleuze and Guattari describe machines working everywhere: machines that produce flows and machines that interrupt them, coupled to one another and to the body.
old.note: Reduced to the book's own opening image.

old.text: The Stanford Encyclopedia article by Daniel Smith, John Protevi and Daniela Voss describes desiring-production as the book's key term, a universal primary process underlying natural, social and psychological reality alike, and stresses two features of it: no subject stands behind the production, and the desire at work is purely positive, organized around no lack.
old.note: The key term, a universal primary process, no subject behind it, purely positive.

old.text: A desiring-machine is binary: a flow and a break in it, as the mouth cuts the flow of milk from the breast.
old.note: The mouth is coupled to the breast, a milk-producing machine; 'cuts' is the entry's gloss, dropped.

old.text: Each break supplies a new flow for the next machine, so that machines link into chains within bodies and between bodies, nature and society, under the formula “and … and then”.
old.note: Chains within and between bodies, nature and society: not confirmed; the formula kept.

old.text: John Protevi's notes on the first chapter stress a feature the authors return to often: desiring-machines run only by breaking down, constantly, which sets them apart from technical machines, which work only when they are in order.
old.note: Desiring-machines work only when they break down; technical machines only when in order.

old.text: The fourth section, “A Materialist Psychiatry”, sets this account against the tradition that defines desire by lack, running in the book's telling from Plato to Lacan.
old.note: The book traces the logic of desire as lack to Plato; 'to Lacan' not confirmed in the pages read.

old.text: For Deleuze and Guattari desire produces the real through passive syntheses of partial objects, flows and bodies, and what desire lacks is a fixed subject.
old.note: 'Passive syntheses of partial objects, flows and bodies' not confirmed.

old.text: Desire is a machine, and its object is another machine connected to it.
old.note: Not found in the pages read.

old.text: Lack is created, planned and organized within social production, and needs are counterproducts of desire.
old.note: Lack created, planned and organized in social production; needs as counterproducts.

old.text: The same production runs through society: social production is desiring-production under determinate conditions, and the social field is invested by desire directly, with no need for sublimation or symbolic mediation.
old.note: Under determinate conditions confirmed; 'no need of mediation' confirmed, 'sublimation' and 'symbolic mediation' not.

old.text: Hence the question the authors call the fundamental problem of political philosophy, which they take from Spinoza and Wilhelm Reich: why people fight for their servitude as if it were their salvation, and how desire can come to desire its own repression.
old.note: The fundamental problem; Spinoza's question, which Reich took up; 'desire its own repression' not confirmed and cut.

old.text: Desiring-production works through three syntheses, which the book treats in turn: the connective synthesis of production, the disjunctive synthesis of recording on the body without organs, and the conjunctive synthesis of consumption, in which a subject is produced as a residue alongside the machines.
The authors name the corresponding energies libido, numen and voluptas.
They compare desiring-production to Spinoza's natura naturans and Nietzsche's will to power.

old.text: The model for the whole account is the schizophrenic's stroll with which the book begins, Büchner's Lenz walking in the mountains among machines of sky, earth and body, living nature as a process of production before any split between man and nature.
old.note: The stroll, Lenz as Büchner reconstructed him; man and nature not two opposite terms.

old.text: Clinical schizophrenia, on their reading, is the result of this process being blocked.

old.text: A phrase Deleuze and Guattari take from Antonin Artaud: in Anti-Oedipus the unproductive surface on which desiring-production is recorded; in A Thousand Plateaus a field of intensities beneath the organism's organization.
The phrase comes from Antonin Artaud's radio work To Have Done with the Judgment of God, recorded in November 1947.
old.note: Made for French radio in late 1947 and cancelled before its February 1948 broadcast; a recording date is not given.

old.text: Deleuze had already used it in The Logic of Sense (1969), where, as the Stanford Encyclopedia article notes, it names the risings and fallings of intensity in an infant's experience.
old.note: The rising and falling intensities are Daniel Stern's image of infant experience; the body without organs names a life of intensities in motion.

old.text: Deleuze and Guattari make it one of the basic concepts of Anti-Oedipus.
In the first chapter the body without organs appears as the third moment of the connective synthesis.
Production stops for a moment and an enormous undifferentiated object forms, unproductive and sterile, the element of antiproduction within production itself.
old.note: Quoted.

old.text: The organized organism, the body arranged by machines, is felt as persecution, and the authors connect this full body with the death instinct and take catatonia as its clinical model.
old.note: The death instinct, catatonia, the persecution apparatus.

old.text: It is then constantly reinserted into production.
Two relations follow.
By repulsion the body without organs pushes the machines away, which the authors call the paranoiac machine.
By attraction it draws them onto itself, so that production seems to emanate from it, which they call the miraculating machine.

It becomes the surface on which production is recorded, the site of the disjunctive synthesis, and the opposition of repulsion and attraction is reconciled in a celibate machine, where a subject is produced in the conjunctive synthesis.
The same structure appears in society.

Social production has its own full body, the socius, which falls back on production, records it and appropriates its surplus, so that production appears to come from it: the earth in territorial societies, the body of the despot in states, capital under capitalism.
old.note: Earth, despot, capital confirmed; 'appropriates its surplus' not confirmed.

old.text: Protevi's notes record the authors' formula that capital is the body without organs of the capitalist.
old.note: Quoted from the book.

old.text: Intensity runs through all of this.

The body without organs is zero intensity, and the subject passes through the states that attraction and repulsion produce on it, bands of intensity, thresholds and gradients; the authors liken it to an egg crossed by axes and gradients, the egg as embryology describes it before organs form.
old.note: Zero intensity, bands, thresholds, gradients; the egg. 'As embryology describes it' not confirmed.

old.text: A Thousand Plateaus devotes its sixth plateau to the question of how one makes oneself a body without organs, dated by the day of Artaud's recording.
old.note: The plateau's title carries the date; that it is the day of the recording is not confirmed.

old.text: There the body without organs is opposed to the organism, one of the strata that organize bodies, and the Stanford Encyclopedia article glosses it as a reservoir of potentials for different patterns of bodily affect.

old.text: The authors present it as a practice of experimentation and warn that hasty destratification can produce emptied or cancerous bodies, so the experiment requires caution.

old.text: The three processes that make up desiring-production in Anti-Oedipus, connective, disjunctive and conjunctive, each with an immanent, legitimate use and a transcendent, illegitimate use that produces Oedipus.
Deleuze and Guattari model their analysis on Kant's critique of reason.
Kant distinguished legitimate uses of the syntheses of consciousness from illegitimate, transcendent uses that generate illusions.
old.note: Kant's own distinction not checked against a source here.

old.text: Anti-Oedipus does the same for the unconscious: each synthesis of desire has an immanent use, which the authors study under the name of schizoanalysis, and a transcendent use, which psychoanalysis imposes when it posits a subject or a family behind the syntheses.
The Stanford Encyclopedia article stresses that subjects are products of the syntheses and never their agents.
The connective synthesis is the production of production, with the formula “and … and then”: machines couple flows and break them, and the energy at work is libido.
Its legitimate use is partial and nonspecific, linking partial objects in open chains.
old.note: Partial confirmed; 'open chains' not.

old.text: Its illegitimate use is global and specific: it refers partial objects to complete objects and whole persons, mother and father, and fixes a sex.
The authors call this the paralogism of extrapolation.
The disjunctive synthesis is the production of recording on the body without organs, with the formula “either … or … or”, and its energy is numen.
Used inclusively and without restriction, it lets the subject pass through every position in a system of permutations.
old.note: Every position in a system of permutations: not confirmed.

old.text: Used exclusively and restrictively, it forces a choice between fixed terms, either man or woman, either parent or child, and the authors name this the paralogism of the double bind, borrowing Gregory Bateson's term.
old.note: Exclusive, restrictive either/or and the double bind confirmed; the examples not.

old.text: The conjunctive synthesis is the production of consumption, with the formula “so it's …”, and its energy is voluptas.
Here a subject is born as a residue beside the machines, defined by the states it passes through.

Its legitimate use is nomadic and polyvocal; its illegitimate use is segregative and biunivocal, fixing one-to-one relations between figures of the social field and the parents of the family triangle, which the authors call the paralogism of application.
Two further paralogisms complete the critique.

Displacement, discussed in the section on social and psychic repression, has the law forbid something and the subject conclude that it desired what was forbidden, so that Oedipus becomes a product of repression.
old.note: Displacement as a falsified image of what is repressed; the entry's account of the law reworded.

old.text: The paralogism of the afterward, in the section on neurosis and psychosis, treats actual factors as mere after-effects of earlier family problems.
Protevi's notes give the section and page ranges for each, and the reading notes from Duke University give the pages where the paralogisms are named.
old.note: The Duke reading notes name no author; dropped as a source.

old.text: The critical practice proposed in Anti-Oedipus: a materialist psychiatry that traces how desire invests the social field directly, set against the Oedipal reductions of psychoanalysis.
Schizoanalysis is the name Deleuze and Guattari give to the practice developed in Anti-Oedipus, which they also call materialist psychiatry.
It treats the unconscious as an aggregate of productive processes of desire and studies the immanent use of the syntheses of the unconscious.

Its starting points are schizophrenia and the transformations capitalism has produced in society, and its target is what the authors regard as the reactionary tendency of psychoanalysis to reduce all desire to the family.
Schizophrenia matters to it as a process.
The schizophrenic process reveals the universal primary production of desire; the clinical schizophrenic, on the Stanford Encyclopedia article's reading, is what results when that process is blocked.

Ronald Bogue's summary, adapted in Protevi's outline, presents the schizophrenic id as a better guide to social desire than the neurotic ego, and treats the individual as a heterogeneous aggregate of parts in social and natural machines.
old.note: Protevi's outline after Bogue is marked 'do not cite'; dropped.

old.text: The critique of psychoanalysis runs through the second chapter.
Freud discovered desiring-production, the authors argue, and then replaced the factory with a theater, staging desire in the family triangle of daddy, mommy and me.
Social repression delegates the repression of desire to the family, and psychic repression makes social repression itself desired.
old.note: The family is the agent social repression delegates; 'makes social repression desired' not confirmed.

old.text: Wilhelm Reich is credited with seeing how social repression works through sexual repression and criticized for failing to carry the analysis of desire far enough.
old.note: Called the true father of materialist psychiatry and faulted for two consequences.

old.text: Their contrast is with the tree and the root, the arborescent model of thought: a single origin, a hierarchy of branches, binary divisions and fixed order, which they find in classical logic, genealogy and the tree diagrams of linguistics.

old.text: The tree, they write, is filiation, while the rhizome is alliance, and its fabric is the conjunction “and … and … and …”.

By the principle of multiplicity, the multiple becomes a substantive with no relation to the One as subject or object.

By asignifying rupture, a rhizome broken at any point starts up again along old lines or new ones; their example is the wasp and the orchid, which form a rhizome as each takes up something of the other.

old.text: In Kafka: Toward a Minor Literature (1975), the literature a minority makes within a major language, marked by the deterritorialization of language, an immediate political charge and a collective value.
Deleuze and Guattari define a minor literature as the literature a minority makes in a major language, as distinct from the literature of a minor language.
Their case is Franz Kafka, a Prague Jew writing in German, the language of a minority amid a Czech population.
old.note: 'Amid a Czech population' not confirmed.

old.text: They give a minor literature three characteristics.
Its language is affected by a high coefficient of deterritorialization.
Everything in it is political, since its cramped space connects each individual affair immediately to politics.
And everything in it takes on a collective value: even the most individual utterance is a collective enunciation.
Sara De Balsi notes that the authors present these features as the revolutionary conditions of any literature within an established one.

The word comes from Kafka's diaries, where he reflects on what he calls small literatures; De Balsi notes that the French adjective “mineure” entered the discussion through Marthe Robert's translation of the diaries in 1954.
Two responses to a deterritorialized language are possible.

One is symbolic reterritorialization, which the authors find in the Prague German writers around Max Brod, who enriched the language with symbolism and dream and reterritorialized it in a Zionist hope, and in Joyce's exuberant overdetermination.
The other is absolute deterritorialization, Kafka's way: to take the poverty of Prague German and push it further, with sobriety, into intensity.
A minor use of language makes one a stranger within one's own language.
A Thousand Plateaus later generalizes the idea of the minor into a becoming open to anyone, and speaks of minor science alongside minor literature.
Critics have since used the concept for writers working in languages not their own; De Balsi applies it to translingual writing.
old.note: De Balsi limits it: not every second-language writer.

old.text: Deleuze's project in Difference and Repetition (1968): to think difference before and apart from identity, freeing it from its subordination to representation.

Difference and Repetition (1968), Deleuze's principal thesis for the doctorat d'État, works through the history of philosophy to isolate two concepts that earlier assumptions had blocked: difference in itself and repetition for itself.
old.note: Primary thesis confirmed; the rest editorial.

old.text: In the preface to the English translation (1994) he called it the first book in which he tried to “do philosophy”.
Ordinarily difference is an empirical relation between two terms that already have their identities.

The Stanford Encyclopedia article describes Deleuze's reversal: identity is produced by a prior relation between differentials, so that difference becomes a transcendental principle, the sufficient reason of empirical diversity, as a difference in electrical potential accounts for a flash of lightning.
old.note: Prior relation between differentials and lightning confirmed; the electrical potential not.

old.text: What blocks this concept is representation, which subordinates difference to a fourfold structure: identity in the concept, opposition between predicates, analogy in judgment and resemblance in perception.

The model is Aristotle's logic of genus and species as Porphyry systematized it, where specific differences such as rational and irrational divide the genus animal, and individuals of a species differ only in ways registered by resemblance.
Deleuze also rejects Hegel's way of thinking difference through contradiction, which carries difference to its extreme only to bring it back under identity.
Against Plato's division of models and copies he sets the simulacrum, and he describes his project as an overturning of Platonism.
Leibniz's differential calculus supplies a model of difference that is affirmed in its own right, with negation as something secondary.
The third chapter attacks the dogmatic image of thought in eight postulates, among them the good nature of thought, common sense, recognition and representation.
Real thinking, on Deleuze's account, starts from an encounter with something that cannot be recognized, which forces the faculties out of their accord.
The Stanford article compares this to the Kantian sublime and its discordant accord of the faculties, leaving thought with a fractured self.
Repetition is distinct from generality, the order of cycles, equalities and laws described by science.
old.note: Generality belongs to the order of laws; cycles not confirmed.

old.text: Deleuze describes repetition as difference without a concept and finds repetition in art, in humor and irony, and in Borges's Pierre Menard, who rewrites Don Quixote word for word.
old.note: Difference without a concept confirmed; Menard and humor not.

old.text: Repetition for itself repeats difference: following his reading of Nietzsche's eternal return, only what differs returns.
Intensity carries the argument into the physical world.

Intensive magnitudes such as temperature cannot be divided without changing in kind, and differences of intensity drive the processes, such as convection in heated water, that produce extended things.
Guides to the book include Joe Hughes's reader's guide (2009), James Williams's critical introduction (2003) and Henry Somers-Hall's study (2013).

old.text: The three passive syntheses of time in chapter 2 of Difference and Repetition: habit, which founds the living present; memory, which grounds it in the pure past; and the eternal return, the empty form of time and the future.
The second chapter of Difference and Repetition, “Repetition for Itself”, describes time as constituted by three syntheses.
They are passive, operating beneath the active syntheses of a conscious subject, and each brings past and future into the present in a different way.
The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy ties the first to habit and the living present, the second to memory and the pure past, and the third to Nietzsche's eternal return and the future.
old.note: The third tied to the eternal return and the future; the eternal return is not called Nietzsche's there.

old.text: The first synthesis is habit.
Taking up Hume's account of how repeated cases produce expectation, Deleuze describes a contraction of successive instants into a living present that retains the past and anticipates the future.
Such contractions happen everywhere in organic life, at the level of cells and organs as much as minds, and he speaks of the many larval selves, or contemplative souls, that these habits constitute.
old.note: Larval subjects and contemplative souls confirmed; cells and organs not in a citable source.

old.text: Habit is the foundation of time.
The second synthesis is memory, after Bergson's Matter and Memory: a pure past that was never present as such, which coexists with every present and makes the present pass.
old.note: Bergson's paradoxes of memory; Matter and Memory not named.

old.text: If habit is the foundation of time, memory is its ground.
Deleuze names it after Mnemosyne, and its literary model is Proust's search for a past preserved in itself.
The third synthesis is the eternal return, the empty form of time.

Deleuze takes Hamlet's “the time is out of joint” for a time freed from cycles and movements, divided by a caesura, an act too big for the self, into a before and an after; Kant's split between the determining I and the determinable self becomes the fractured I of this time.
old.note: Out of joint, caesura, before and after, the fractured I; Hamlet, the act too big and Kant not confirmed.

old.text: Nietzsche's eternal return is its content: the return of difference alone, which ungrounds the earlier syntheses and opens the future.

Deleuze discusses Freud in the same chapter, setting habit beside the binding of excitations that founds the pleasure principle, memory beside Eros and Mnemosyne, and the third synthesis beside a desexualized death instinct, Thanatos.

old.text: Deleuze's distinction, drawn from Bergson, between the virtual, real conditions of genesis structured as differential multiplicities, and the actual things and states of affairs that emerge from them.
For Deleuze the virtual is fully real.
It is the condition of the genesis of real experience, and its relation to what it conditions is actualization.
He takes the concept from Bergson and adopts a phrase from Proust for its status: real without being actual, ideal without being abstract.
old.note: Bergsonism confirmed; the Proust phrase not.

old.text: The Stanford Encyclopedia article stresses the contrast with possibility: the possible is realized and resembles the real it becomes, while the virtual is actualized by processes that create something unlike it.
old.note: Actualized, never awaiting realization; resemblance of the possible not confirmed.

old.text: Because the ground cannot resemble what it grounds, the virtual must be purely differential.
Deleuze calls its structures Ideas or multiplicities, taking multiplicity from Bergson as a noun, which replaces the dialectic of the one and the many with a typology of multiplicities.

An Idea is a system of differential elements, differential relations between them and singularities; the Stanford article's examples include the phonemes of a language, each defined by its differences from others, and a hurricane, explained by its Idea and caused by actual wind currents.

Deleuze distinguishes differentiation, the determination of the virtual content of an Idea, from differenciation, the actualization of that content in particular species and parts, and writes the whole process as different/ciation.
In differentiation alternatives coexist; in differenciation one path is taken.
Between the two lies intensity.

The Stanford article describes three registers, virtual, intensive and actual: beneath actual things are impersonal individuations, intensive processes of formation, and beneath these are pre-individual singularities, thresholds in virtual fields.
Drawing on Gilbert Simondon's account of crystallization, Deleuze treats individuation as the resolution of a metastable field, as crystals precipitate from a supersaturated solution.

A Thousand Plateaus keeps the three registers under new names, the Earth for the virtual, consistency for the intensive and the strata for the actual, and the Stanford article notes that nothing ever fully instantiates either the pure actual or the pure virtual, which makes the authors process philosophers.
old.note: Now quoted.

old.text: The thesis that being is said in one and the same sense of everything of which it is said, which Deleuze takes from Duns Scotus, Spinoza and Nietzsche as the basis of a philosophy of difference.
Medieval philosophers debated how “being” applies to God and creatures.

If it is said equivocally, in different senses, nothing can be known of God from creatures; Thomas Aquinas held that it is said by analogy; John Duns Scotus argued that it is univocal, said in one sense of everything that is.
old.note: Scotus's argument concerns concepts drawn from creatures.

old.text: Deleuze takes up Scotus's thesis and declares, in the first chapter of Difference and Repetition, that there has only ever been one ontological proposition: being is univocal.
Univocity, for Deleuze, means that being is said in a single and same sense of all its individuating differences.
Its sense is one; what it is said of differs.

This lets difference be thought within being itself, with no need to divide being into genera and species, which is why the Stanford Encyclopedia article calls univocity the key to a philosophy of difference.
He presents its history in three moments.
Scotus thought univocal being in a neutral, abstract form.
Spinoza made it an object of affirmation: a single substance expressed in its attributes and modes, with being said in one sense of substance and of its modes.
Nietzsche's eternal return completes it, with being said of becoming and of difference.
The second and third moments shape Deleuze's books on Spinoza, Expressionism in Philosophy: Spinoza (1968) and Spinoza: Practical Philosophy (1970; second edition 1981).
old.note: Spinoza and the Problem of Expression as the secondary thesis; Practical Philosophy not checked.

old.text: The Stanford article describes the result as a Spinozism minus substance: a purely modal or differential universe in which differences are differences in degrees of power.
old.note: Now quoted.

old.text: It distinguishes puissance, a body's immanent power to act, from pouvoir, power as domination.

old.text: On a univocal view, every being, however small, is equally being.

old.text: The view that meaning and identity arise from differential relations within a system. Elements mean nothing in isolation; they mean by their differences from other elements.

Lévi-Strauss “structuralized” anthropology, beginning with The Elementary Structures of Kinship (1949); Lacan drew on Saussure and on structural linguists such as Roman Jakobson to reread Freud, holding that the unconscious is structured like a language; Barthes analyzed fashion, myth and narrative; and Althusser read Marx structurally.
